analysis.one_liner: Replaces private health insurance, Medicare, and Medicaid with a government-run universal health plan in every state.
analysis.headline: The single-payer bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on March 25, 2009 and never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Sanders's bill would have created a state-run health plan covering every U.S. resident—covering hospital care, doctors, prescription drugs, dental, mental health, vision, and long-term care—for which providers could bill nothing beyond the program's payment. It would have ended Medicare, Medicaid, CHIP, federal employee health coverage, and military civilian health coverage as we know them, and banned the sale of insurance that duplicates covered benefits. It would have been financed by new payroll and income taxes paid into a federal trust fund. The bill never received a hearing, a vote, or a cosponsor in the Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident would gain guaranteed comprehensive coverage with no premiums, deductibles, or balance billing, including benefits many current plans exclude: dental care, eyeglasses, hearing aids, mental health and substance abuse treatment, and home- and community-based long-term care. People with employer coverage would no longer lose it when changing jobs, and the sickest and lowest-income Americans would no longer face medical bills or be uninsurable.
analysis.who_benefits_short: All U.S. residents, especially the uninsured

how_it_helps.text: Every U.S. citizen, national, and lawful resident would be entitled to comprehensive coverage—including prescription drugs, dental care, mental health services, vision, hearing aids, and home- and community-based long-term care—with no charge for covered services and no balance billing (Sec. 201).

It would replace the separate Medicare, Medicaid, SCHIP, FEHB, and CHAMPUS programs with one system in each state, so nobody loses coverage when they change or lose a job, and benefits follow people across state lines (Sec. 104).

States would pay hospitals through global budgets and set drug prices nationally, replacing the current mix of private billing and negotiation that drives up prices; a national health security budget would set total federal and state spending on care (Sec. 601, 611, 615).
It would prohibit the sale of duplicative health insurance and require providers to accept the program's payment as full payment, eliminating deductibles, copays, and out-of-network charges.

analysis.who_pays: Employers would pay a new payroll tax and individuals a new health care income tax, replacing the premiums and out-of-pocket costs they pay today. Private insurers would lose the market for duplicative coverage, hospitals and doctors would be paid under state-set global budgets and fee schedules instead of negotiated charges, and the drug industry would face nationally set prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers via new payroll and income taxes

drawbacks.text: The bill bans the sale of any health insurance that duplicates covered benefits (Sec. 201(c)) and repeals existing employer-based coverage structures under ERISA, so the entire private health insurance business in each state would end, and the millions of jobs and employer benefit arrangements built around it would be disrupted.

Financing would shift to new employer payroll taxes and a health care income tax flowing into a federal trust fund (Title VIII), meaning households and employers would pay through taxes what they currently pay through premiums—still a large, visible cost even if lower overall.

Hospitals would be paid via state-approved global budgets and doctors via fee schedules, replacing negotiated payments; providers argue such payment systems can constrain investment and access to care, and the bill itself acknowledges transition problems by requiring an annual report on them (Sec. 401(g)(2)(L)).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—universal coverage with no premiums or deductibles, including dental, mental health, and long-term care—would be substantial for ordinary people, and consolidating all payment into one public system per state is a genuine mechanism for cutting administrative overhead and bargaining drug prices down. The costs are real: new payroll and income taxes would replace premiums, and the transition would be disruptive for employers who now buy insurance, for health industries that live off billing complexity, and for workers in insurance administration. The bill's design choices (global hospital budgets, global drug purchasing) would put heavy pressure on provider and drug-company revenues, which supporters count as savings and critics warn could affect access to care. The serious drawback is political: with no cosponsors, the bill was never seriously considered, and the eventual 2010 law took a far more incremental route.

outcome.mechanism: Sanders introduced it, the Senate sent it to the Finance Committee, and the committee never acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 25, 2009, read twice, and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
The action history shows no further activity: no hearings, no committee markup, no floor vote, and no reintroduction of substance before the 111th Congress ended.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor, so the bill had no demonstrated coalition of support in the chamber.

The bill text shows it was a full single-payer proposal: universal entitlement to comprehensive benefits, elimination of Medicare, Medicaid, SCHIP, FEHB, and CHAMPUS, a ban on duplicative private insurance, and new payroll and income taxes into a federal trust fund.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The private health insurance industry, hospital systems, and drug companies that would have lost payment power under the bill are better off because it never moved; Congress instead debated smaller incremental reforms.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers, drug companies, and hospital billing interests

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to create a state-based single-payer health program replacing Medicare, Medicaid, SCHIP, FEHB, and CHAMPUS.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no action—no hearing, markup, or vote—leaving it to die in committee.

against.name: Health insurance and pharmaceutical industry
against.what_they_did: Lobbied heavily during the 2009 health care debate against a public, government-run coverage model that would displace private insurance.

against.name: Senate Republican caucus
against.what_they_did: Opposed single-payer legislation during the 2009 health reform debate.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so no party positions on the bill itself are recorded; the eventual 2010 health law took a different, market-based route.

industries.note: States would be required to prohibit the sale of any insurance duplicating covered benefits, eliminating the core market for health insurance in every state.
Providers would gain guaranteed universal payment for every patient but would be paid through state-set global budgets and fee schedules rather than negotiated charges, ending balance billing.
Drug payments would be set by the Standards Board under a national budget rather than negotiated with private payers, removing a major source of pricing leverage.
Employers would stop paying premiums but would face a new payroll tax, and would be barred from providing duplicate coverage except for extra benefits on top of the program.
